name: Deathcore
about: Deathcore crossed death metal's blast beats, tremolo riffs and guttural vocals with metalcore's breakdowns, and made the breakdown the point. Its roots lie in early-2000s bands like The Red Chord and Despised Icon, who mixed grind and slam with hardcore, but the style properly arrived around 2006 and 2007 through MySpace, when Suicide Silence, Job for a Cowboy, Whitechapel and Carnifex found a teenage audience that metal's old guard loathed. The sound is downtuned, chug-heavy and theatrically brutal, with pig squeals, open-note breakdowns and triggered drums; the production is enormous. Derided for a decade, it matured in the 2010s as Thy Art Is Murder and Fit for an Autopsy tightened the songwriting, and Lorna Shore's symphonic, Will Ramos-fronted records in the 2020s made it, improbably, extreme metal's most popular wing.

artists.name: Job for a Cowboy
artists.why: the Doom EP started a craze

artists.name: Bring Me the Horizon
artists.why: started in deathcore, ended in stadiums

albums.title: This Is Exile
albums.why: Three guitars, Phil Bozeman's bottomless growl and genuine death-metal craft made the Knoxville band's second album the style's first fully convincing record.

albums.title: Pain Remains
albums.why: Will Ramos's inhuman vocal range and a symphonic, black-metal-tinged scope on a closing trilogy that pushed deathcore to its most ambitious point yet.

albums.title: Fused Together in Revolving Doors
albums.why: Grindcore, death metal and metalcore collided on the Massachusetts band's debut, the record most often cited as deathcore's year zero.

albums.title: The Ills of Modern Man
albums.why: Two vocalists trading pig squeals and roars over slam-derived riffs, the Montreal band's third album is the sound at its most technical and nasty.

albums.title: The Cleansing
albums.why: Mitch Lucker's high-low vocals and Unanswered's breakdowns made the Riverside band's debut Century Media's best-selling first album at the time.

albums.title: Hate
albums.why: Reign of Darkness and a blast-heavy, death-metal-first approach made the Australians the band that gave deathcore back its credibility.

albums.title: The Great Collapse
albums.why: Producer-guitarist Will Putney's band wrote about climate and politics over Gojira-sized grooves, a record with actual songs underneath the heaviness.

albums.title: The Valley
albums.why: Bozeman's clean singing and lyrics about his mother's illness made the band's seventh album its most personal and musically broad.

albums.title: Oh What the Future Holds
albums.why: Melodic choruses, sludge passages and the band's tightest songwriting on a record that argued deathcore could be a mature form.

albums.title: We Are Gathered Here Today...
albums.why: North Carolina's Glass Casket, with future Between the Buried and Me members, mixed technical death metal and hardcore before the style had a name.

albums.title: The Healing Process
albums.why: The Montreal band's second album fixed the dual-vocal, slam-meets-hardcore formula that MySpace bands would copy two years later.

albums.title: The Price of Existence
albums.why: Melodic leads and Hernan Hermida's vocal range gave the Oakland band's second album more musicality than most of the first wave.

albums.title: Genesis
albums.why: After the scene-defining Doom EP, the Arizona band's first album moved toward straight death metal and kept the momentum going.

albums.title: Dead in My Arms
albums.why: Raw, breakdown-heavy and gothic in tone, the San Diego band's debut is the MySpace era in a single record.

albums.artist: Through the Eyes of the Dead
albums.title: Malice
albums.why: South Carolina's Through the Eyes of the Dead wrapped deathcore around melodic death metal leads on a tight, underrated second album.

albums.title: Continent
albums.why: Vincent Bennett's misanthropy over glacial, downtuned chugs, the Massachusetts band's definitive statement of nihilist heaviness.

albums.title: Suicide Season
albums.why: The Sheffield band's second album widened their deathcore with melody and Chase and Status remixes, the hinge before they left the style behind.

albums.title: Depths
albums.why: Adam Warren's cavernous vocals and bottom-heavy breakdowns on a Chicago debut that defined deathcore's slower, slam-indebted wing.

albums.title: No Time to Bleed
albums.why: Machine's production and nu-metal grooves broadened the debut's attack; the band's most commercially successful record with Lucker.

albums.title: [id]
albums.why: Marc Okubo's tapping, djent-style riffs over deathcore rhythms on the Chicago band's breakthrough third album.

albums.title: Desolation of Eden
albums.why: The Salt Lake City band's debut is breakdown-driven deathcore at its most unapologetic, hugely popular and critically scorned in equal measure.

albums.title: The Unconquerable Dark
albums.why: Hull's Black Tongue slowed deathcore to a doom crawl with symphonic flourishes, the heaviest and bleakest record in the style's British wing.

albums.title: Melancholy
albums.why: Orchestral arrangements and Ben Duerr's vocals on the Connecticut band's third album, which anticipated the symphonic turn Lorna Shore made famous.

albums.title: Välde
albums.why: Buster Odeholm's Swedish project combined djent, doom and deathcore into a record of oppressive, downtuned atmosphere.
